title: What's Behind the Flap About "Maus"
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Wexler argues that the Tennessee school board's removal of Maus from its eighth-grade curriculum is better understood as a curriculum story than a simple censorship story. The district adopted EL Education because Tennessee approved only literacy curricula that build background knowledge, and Maus is the centrepiece of that curriculum's Holocaust module. She uses the board's own meeting minutes to show that members objected to specific language and imagery, not to teaching the Holocaust, and that a supervisor's cow-nutrition paragraph was meant to show why students need knowledge to comprehend text. Her move is to defend the knowledge-building approach to reading comprehension against skills-based instruction while urging readers to understand, rather than demonise, the board. She concludes that swapping in a different text, or choosing a better-aligned approved curriculum, would serve students better than abandoning the module and the curriculum reform with it.
points: Skills-focused comprehension instruction (find the main idea) leaves students without the knowledge and vocabulary needed to read complex texts, which is why Tennessee approved knowledge-building curricula.
The cow-nutrition paragraph demonstrates that comprehension depends on topic knowledge, a point the board seemingly did not grasp when it suggested simply rewriting the module.

Because the two-month module is built around Maus, removing the book likely means dropping the Holocaust unit rather than replacing one text, and writing curriculum is hard for districts to do themselves.
Alternatives such as Night or a state-approved curriculum better matched to local values could preserve knowledge-building without the conflict.
Not all book challenges are equal: orchestrated Moms for Liberty challenges differ from sincere local objections, and demonising the latter risks a return to ineffective teaching.
quotes: Equally crucial is the way schools have taught reading comprehension. Most literacy curricula have been organized around supposed comprehension skills like “finding the main idea.” Teachers are guided to focus on having students master the skills, with the content treated as secondary.

The problem with that approach, as Tennessee and other states have recognized, is that most students never get a chance to acquire the academic knowledge and vocabulary that would enable them to understand more complex texts.

What we’re finding,” he continued, “is that students can’t have rigorous learning on topics they know little to nothing about. When we jump from one topic to the next, all our time is spent just figuring out words and what they meant.

Unfortunately, it’s not that simple. The whole two-month module is built around Maus and the idea of graphic novels, with lesson plans and discussion questions. Writing curriculum is a complex task that most administrators and teachers haven’t been trained to do.

But that shouldn’t prevent us from recognizing that all children, including those in McMinn, deserve a meaningful education. If our schools fail to provide the knowledge and vocabulary that enable people to understand a newspaper and follow current events—as has been the case for far too long—all of us living in a democracy will suffer.

The complaints there seem to be sincere and home-grown. Demonizing those who raise them is unlikely to result in anything but more political polarization—and perhaps a return to teaching approaches that simply don’t work.
